questions.q: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration. The ratio of the distances covered in the $1$st, $2$nd and $3$rd seconds is:
questions.solution:
Distance in the $n$th second is $s_n = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$.

With $u = 0$ this is $s_n = \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$.

$s_1 : s_2 : s_3 = 1 : 3 : 5$.

This is the odd-number rule Galileo found rolling balls down an inclined plane. Do not confuse it with total distance from rest, which goes as $1 : 4 : 9$.

questions.q: A projectile is thrown with speed $u$ at angle $\theta$. Its horizontal range is maximum when $\theta$ equals:
questions.solution:
Range $R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}$.

$R$ is largest when $\sin 2\theta = 1$, that is $2\theta = 90^\circ$, so $\theta = \mathbf{45^\circ}$.

A useful companion fact: $\theta$ and $(90^\circ - \theta)$ give the **same** range, because $\sin 2\theta = \sin(180^\circ - 2\theta)$.

questions.q: Rain falls vertically at $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. A man walks east at $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. He should hold his umbrella at an angle to the vertical of:
questions.solution:
In the man's frame, the rain's velocity is $\vec{v}_{\text{rain}} - \vec{v}_{\text{man}}$.

The rain has velocity $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ downward; subtracting the man's $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ eastward adds a $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ **westward** component to the apparent rain.

So the rain appears to come from ahead of him — from the east — at an angle $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$ from the vertical.

The umbrella must be tilted **towards the east**, into the apparent rain: $\mathbf{\tan^{-1}(3/4)}$ towards the east.

questions.q: The area under a velocity-time graph gives:
questions.solution:
Velocity is $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$, so $x = \displaystyle\int v\,dt$ — which is exactly the area under the $v$-$t$ curve.

It gives **displacement**, not distance: area below the time axis counts as negative. To get distance travelled, take the area of the magnitude $|v|$.

By the same logic the **slope** of a $v$-$t$ graph is acceleration.

questions.q: At the highest point of a projectile's path, its:
options: Vertical component of velocity is zero
Horizontal component of velocity is zero
questions.solution:
At the top the projectile has stopped rising and has not yet begun to fall, so $v_y = 0$.

The horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ is unchanged throughout — nothing acts horizontally.

The acceleration is $g$ downward at **every** point of the flight, including the top. That is the standard trap in this question.

questions.q: A car moving at $v$ is brought to rest in a distance $s$ by a constant retarding force. If its speed is doubled, the stopping distance becomes:
questions.solution:
Using $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$ with final velocity zero:

$0 = u^{2} - 2as \Rightarrow s = \dfrac{u^{2}}{2a}$.

So $s \propto u^{2}$ for a fixed retardation.

Doubling the speed gives $2^{2} = \mathbf{4s}$.

This is the physics behind every road-safety campaign about speed.

questions.q: Two trains, $120\ \text{m}$ and $80\ \text{m}$ long, move towards each other at $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The time to cross each other completely is:
questions.solution:
Moving towards each other, relative speed $= 20 + 30 = 50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

To pass completely, the relative displacement is the sum of the lengths:

$120 + 80 = 200\ \text{m}$.

$t = \dfrac{200}{50} = \mathbf{4\ \text{s}}$.

questions.q: A stone is thrown horizontally from a tower. Neglecting air resistance, the time it takes to reach the ground depends on:
options: The height of the tower only
Both the speed and the height
questions.solution:
The vertical and horizontal motions are independent.

Vertically the stone starts with $u_y = 0$ and falls freely:

$h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2} \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

The horizontal speed appears nowhere in that expression — it sets **where** the stone lands, not **when**.

A stone thrown horizontally and one simply dropped from the same height hit the ground together.

questions.q: A particle's position is $x = 3t^{2} - 2t + 5$ (SI units). Its acceleration is:
questions.solution:
$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 6t - 2$

$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \mathbf{6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}}$.

The acceleration is constant — as it must be, since $x$ is a quadratic in $t$.

questions.q: A ball is projected at $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, find the time of flight in seconds.
For the ball in the previous question ($u = 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\theta = 30^\circ$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$), find the maximum height reached, in metres.
A body dropped from rest falls for $3\ \text{s}$. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, how far does it fall, in metres?

A boat can row at $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in still water. A river $100\ \text{m}$ wide flows at $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. If the boat heads straight across (perpendicular to the bank), how far downstream, in metres, does it land?
questions.solution:
Heading straight across, the crossing time is set by the boat's own speed:

$t = \dfrac{100}{5} = 20\ \text{s}$.

The current carries it downstream throughout that time:

drift $= 3 \times 20 = \mathbf{60\ \text{m}}$.

Note the crossing time does **not** depend on the current when the boat heads perpendicular — the current has no component across the river.

questions.q: A particle moves with velocity $v = 4t$ (SI units). Find the displacement, in metres, between $t = 0$ and $t = 3\ \text{s}$.
questions.solution:
$x = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{3} 4t\,dt = \left[2t^{2}\right]_{0}^{3} = 2(9) - 0 = \mathbf{18\ \text{m}}$.

Geometrically this is the area of a triangle under the straight line $v = 4t$: base $3\ \text{s}$, height $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, area $\tfrac{1}{2}(3)(12) = 18$.

questions.q: A projectile is launched with speed $u$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. Derive expressions for its **time of flight**, **maximum height** and **horizontal range**, stating the assumptions. Hence show that the range is the same for $\theta$ and $(90^\circ - \theta)$.
questions.solution:
**Assumptions.** Gravity is uniform and vertical, air resistance is neglected, and the ground is level so the projectile lands at the height it was launched from.

**Setting up.** Resolve the initial velocity:

horizontal $u_x = u\cos\theta$, constant, since nothing acts horizontally

vertical $u_y = u\sin\theta$, with acceleration $-g$

**Time of flight.** The projectile returns to $y = 0$:

$0 = u\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2} = t\left(u\sin\theta - \tfrac{1}{2}gt\right)$

Rejecting $t = 0$ (the launch):

$T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$

**Maximum height.** At the top $v_y = 0$. Using $v_y^{2} = u_y^{2} - 2gH$:

$0 = u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta - 2gH \Rightarrow H = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{2g}$

**Horizontal range.** The horizontal speed is constant, so

$R = u\cos\theta \times T = u\cos\theta \times \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2u^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$

Using $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta$:

$R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}$

**Complementary angles.** Replace $\theta$ by $(90^\circ - \theta)$:

$R' = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin\left(2(90^\circ - \theta)\right)}{g} = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin(180^\circ - 2\theta)}{g}$

Since $\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin x$, this is $\dfrac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g} = R$.

So $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ give the same range, as do $20^\circ$ and $70^\circ$ — though the higher angle always takes longer and goes higher.
